Rav Sherevya places the death after midday but the father at death’s door when midday arrived.
Rav Ashi uses Rabbi Shimon’s view that a living animal is not permanently deferred.
Ravina has the designation and death both after midday, so the midday threshold did not fix this animal.
Mixed offerings graze until blemished; the owner buys each required type at the highest animal’s value and pays any shortfall.
Rabbi Shimon lets groups of priests eat a Paschal animal mixed with firstborn animals.
The Gemara begins discussing the mishna’s mixed offerings.

ranges.en: Eating the mixed firstborn animals by the Paschal deadline may cause sacrificial meat to become invalid prematurely.
Rabbi Shimon accepts that consequence, as when he applies the stricter guilt-offering rules to mixed peace offerings.

How do they handle a Paschal animal mixed with firstborn animals?
Rava waits for blemishes, transfers the Paschal sanctity to a new animal, and has priests eat the originals as blemished firstborns.
A group sends an agent to find and slaughter its lost Paschal animal but also slaughters a replacement.
If the agent’s animal was slaughtered first, he and the group eat from it.
If the group’s animal was first, the group eats its own and the agent eats his.

Each group conditionally withdraws and registers the visiting member according to which animal it owns.
The same procedure extends to several groups by exchanging representatives.

ranges.en: The mishna bars eating near minḥa on Passover eve and requires reclining and four cups even for a poor person.

A delayed havdala does not include the fire blessing.

ranges.en: Rav’s reported ruling says one who washed hands should not recite kiddush before eating.

Does tasting before havdala likewise prevent reciting havdala?
Rav Huna says havdala may still be recited.
Rav Asi holds that tasting does prevent havdala.
At Rav Asi’s home Rav Yirmeya nevertheless made havdala after accidentally tasting food.
Rav Asi’s wife notes that her husband does not follow that practice.
Rav Asi says the guest follows his own teacher’s view.
One report of Shmuel says tasting prevents both kiddush and havdala.
Another report of Shmuel permits both after tasting.

ranges.en: Rava permits kiddush or havdala after tasting, daytime makeup kiddush, and delayed havdala during the following week.

When wine is unavailable, Ameimar declines beer, waits overnight without eating, then makes havdala on wine.
On a later visit he treats local beer as the region’s customary drink and makes havdala over it.
His conduct shows havdala in prayer does not replace a cup, eating must wait, and delayed havdala is possible.

Rav Hisda says even better beers had no resolved permission, making date beer still less suitable.
Perhaps the restriction applies only to kiddush, not havdala?
Rav Hisda and a separate report of Shmuel bar both kiddush and havdala over that beer.
Rabbi tastes a richly soaked date beer and initially praises it as fit for kiddush and song.
Its later digestive effect changes his assessment.
Rav Yosef and Rava express aversion to drinking beer.
Rava criticizes beer kiddush; Rav teases Rav Huna for using beer after beginning to sell it.

Beer and water plainly receive their ordinary beverage blessing.
Abaye limits the second clause to the cup accompanying Grace after Meals.
A baraita forbids beer for kiddush, while a named tradition permits it.

Rav Huna and Rav Giddel require a cheekful for fulfillment.
Rav Nahman insists on identifying Giddel precisely to compare his rulings consistently.
Does the mishna’s pre-minḥa eating ban mean the greater or lesser minḥa?

ranges.en: Or does the ban begin near lesser minḥa to preserve appetite for matza at night?

This seems noteworthy if the ban begins near lesser minḥa.

The initial inference favors lesser minḥa.

A verse about preparing soil provides an allusion to preparing the appetite.

He begins citing proof that wine stimulates appetite; the citation continues on 108a.

108a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Extra wine may be drunk between early seder cups; if wine filled the stomach, this would spoil appetite for matza, so wine stimulates it.
Rav Sheshet fasts all Passover eve.
Does he take the mishna’s ban to begin near greater minḥa to avoid missing the Paschal offering?
That reading could rely on ben Beteira, who permits slaughter from the morning by reading “between evenings” broadly.
Rav Sheshet may simply have needed to fast to preserve appetite for the nighttime meal.
The reclining rule applies to matza but not bitter herbs.

They concern the first versus last two cups, but which pair requires reclining is disputed.
One view reclines for the first cups because freedom is beginning, not for the later cups.
Another view reclines for the later cups when freedom is realized, not for the first cups.
Since neither allocation is settled, all four cups require reclining.
Lying on the back or right side does not count; right-side reclining also risks choking.
The text distinguishes a wife, an important woman, and a son regarding reclining in a family setting.
Must a student recline in a teacher’s presence?
Abaye recalls reclining with Rabba, but Rav Yosef later invokes reverence for a teacher to exempt students.
A baraita requires even a student with his teacher to recline.
It concerns an apprentice with a craft teacher.
Must a server recline?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says a server who eats matza reclining fulfills the obligation, implying otherwise he does not.
The server therefore must recline.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi obligates women in the four cups; the reason continues on 108b.

108b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Women share the obligation because they too were included in the Exodus miracle.
Shmuel describes the wine quantity and says undiluted, combined, or shared cups can still fulfill an obligation.

Rav says drinking all four at once fulfills wine drinking but not four distinct cups.
Sharing a cup counts only if the person himself drinks most of it.
A baraita requires a quarter-log per cup, seemingly conflicting with Shmuel’s measure for dilution.
Both measures agree: undiluted wine for each cup is diluted to a quarter-log.
Rabbi Yehuda requires recognizable wine taste and color.
Rava cites a verse describing wine’s red appearance.
A baraita includes men, women, and children in the four cups.
Rabbi Yehuda questions wine’s benefit for children and begins suggesting a different provision.

109a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Snacks are given to children before Passover night so they remain awake and ask questions.
Rabbi Eliezer advises moving the matza meal along to keep children engaged.
Rabbi Akiva ends study early on Passover eve for children’s rest, and before Yom Kippur for their meals.
A baraita grounds the duty to bring festival joy to one’s household in the verse commanding rejoicing.
One proposal is to provide wine.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes what household members enjoy, with wine and regionally preferred clothes as examples.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira links Temple-era joy to eating sacrificial meat.
Without the Temple he links festival joy to wine through a psalm.
Rabbi Yitzhak identifies a Tzippori measure used to calculate the Passover quarter-log.
Rabbi Yohanan identifies a Tiberias vessel whose excess over a newer measure equals a quarter-log.
Rav Hisda gives dimensions for a container holding the Torah’s quarter-log.
A ritual-bath derivation requires unimpeded immersion of the entire body in water.
How much water meets that requirement?

109b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Sages give a cubit-by-cubit, three-cubit-deep bath as forty se’ah.
Rav Ashi reports a suggestion that the Temple table was assembled from detachable parts.
A firmly assembled table seems too large for immersion in a minimal cubit-wide bath.
Why could it not be immersed in Solomon’s large sea?
Rabbi Hiyya says that sea held the volume of 150 purification baths.
How could the Sages require four cups if an even number of drinks was considered dangerous?
A baraita warns against consuming or performing acts in pairs.
Rav Nahman reads Passover night as protected from harmful spirits.
Rava says the Grace-after-Meals cup counts toward the obligation but not toward the feared pair.
Ravina begins an answer based on four distinct expressions of freedom, continued on 110a.

110a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ravina treats each seder cup as a separate command, so the four are not counted as a dangerous pair.
Why warn against intimacy twice if a second act involves a fresh decision?
Abaye reads the warning as avoiding intimacy even once after eating or drinking in pairs, lest weakness increase the feared harm.
A baraita puts responsibility for the feared harm of paired drinking on the drinker.
Rav Yehuda says seeing the marketplace between cups breaks the pair.
Rav Ashi describes someone who stepped out between cups.
The concern is said to apply to travel rather than remaining at home.
Rabbi Zeira and Rav Pappa compare sleeping and visiting the bathroom to travel.
Accounts of Rava, Abaye, and Rav Nahman show care about cup counts even indoors.
The text treats prominent people as a special case.
Ulla says ten cups do not carry the feared pairs risk.
He cites ten cups instituted for a mourner’s house as evidence the Sages would not require danger.
The preceding view still treats eight cups as a pair.
Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna use the priestly blessing’s “peace” to exempt eight.
Their view still treats six as a pair.
Rabba and Rav Yosef use “be gracious” in the blessing to exempt six.
Their view still treats four as a pair.
Abaye and Rava use “keep you” to exempt four.
Rava lets scholars depart after four cups and attributes a reported injury to a different cause.
Rav Yosef reports a demon’s account that the king over paired acts does not harm.
An alternate account argues that such a king can act without restraint.
Rav Pappa reports distinctions between the feared harm of two and four cups and between intent and accident.
What remedy does the text give for accidentally leaving after an even number?
It describes holding crossed thumbs and answering an imagined voice with successive odd counts.
A story extends that counting contest until the alleged spirit bursts.
Ameimar reports the beginning of an incantation attributed to a witch leader; it continues on the next daf.

110b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The reported incantation against witches concludes.
The text contrasts western indifference to pairs with Rav Dimi’s concern even for marks on a barrel.
It says concern may affect the perceived risk, while still counseling caution.
Rav Dimi reports a tradition about certain paired foods and a broader decree because an unnamed fourth item is uncertain.
The earlier numerical exemptions are limited to spirits; the text still voices concern about witchcraft.
A story describes a man visiting his former wife’s wine shop while trying to track paired drinks.
After losing count, the story attributes his death to her sorcery and a paired departure.
Rav Avira exempts manufactured plates and loaves from the pairs concern, unlike naturally completed foods.
The text lists exemptions for a store, a changed decision, a guest, and most women, with an exception for a prominent woman.
A spiced wine drink is said to count only toward a favorable number.
Two reports disagree whether uncertainty about pairs calls for a strict or lenient count.
Rav Yosef distinguishes whether wine or beer is the later drink in a three-cup count.
A purity-law mnemonic compares combining a stricter or more lenient item.
Rav Nahman differentiates cups before and during a meal for the counting rule.
Rav Mesharshiya argues the drinker’s total, rather than the table, should settle the count.
He instead accepts that two meal cups do not combine with a cup after the table is removed.
A reported incident is invoked for the table distinction.
Shmuel begins a rule about diluted drinks that continues on 111a.

111a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel exempts diluted drinks other than water from the paired-cup count; Rabbi Yohanan includes water.
Rav Pappa limits the water dispute to mixing hot with cold; matching temperatures do not count as dilution.
Reish Lakish lists four acts that he says expose a person to danger from spirits.
The palm-and-wall concern is limited to a gap narrower than four cubits.
Even then, the concern applies only when no alternate path exists.
Passing between palms is exempted when a public route separates them.
Borrowed water is said to pose a concern only when a child borrowed it.
The concern is further limited to a field rather than a city.
Even in a field, wine and beer are excluded.
The spilled-water warning is limited when dirt or spittle has not interrupted it.
Sunlight or many passersby are said to remove that concern.
Riding a donkey while wearing shoes is also given as protection.
The text retains concern about sorcery despite these conditions and cites a story of injury.
A baraita warns against passing between certain people, animals, or palms in either direction.
What remedy does the baraita offer if such a crossing occurs?
Rav Pappa suggests reciting verses framed by “God” or “no.”
The text attributes feared harm or a quarrel to a menstruating woman crossing between two men.
It repeats the verse-based remedy.
The text alleges sorcery when two women face one another across a crossroads.
What does it suggest for a passerby?
It suggests another route or passing with a companion while holding hands.
Without a companion it supplies an incantation naming alleged spirits.
The text attributes a feared sexual effect to meeting a woman returning from ritual immersion.
It suggests reciting a verse from Psalms as the remedy.
Rav Yitzhak applies a psalm about walking through danger to sleeping under a palm or moon shadow.
A second palm’s shadow is said to remove the palm-tree concern.
A baraita warns about the shadow even in a courtyard; without the second shadow, why mention a courtyard?
It infers that a courtyard remains a concern even with the second shadow.
The moon-shadow warning is limited to the shadow’s position late in the month.

111b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The text attributes illness to using a palm stump or crossing over a palm tree.
It limits the crossing warning when the person’s legs rest on the tree.
Several tree and other shadows are listed as dangerous in the text.
A rule relates the feared danger to branches and hard wood, with a named exception.
A tale says that exceptional tree harmed the alleged spirits rather than people.
Rav Ashi reports that Rav Kahana avoided all such shadows.
The text names spirits said to inhabit particular trees or roofs, for use in amulets.
It describes a caper-bush spirit as eyeless, affecting the suggested response.
A story describes a scholar fleeing a spirit that then destroys a palm tree.
A sorb tree near a town is said to contain sixty spirits, a detail used for an amulet.
A tale contrasts an insufficient amulet for one spirit with an amulet for sixty.
The text describes two kinds of the alleged ketev spirit, before and after noon.
A story says Abaye changed which companion walked on his left when he perceived danger.
Rav Pappa asks why Abaye was less concerned for him.
Abaye says Rav Pappa’s favorable circumstances would protect him.
The text gives a season and shadow locations associated with the alleged spirits.
Rav Yosef lists three practices he says damage eyesight.
A proverb links hanging bread with poverty, while exempting hanging meat or fish.
The text also associates bran and crumbs with poverty and names spirits for food and poverty.
It links a plate on a jug with poverty, water drunk from a plate with eye pain, and unwashed cress with fear.

112a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The text attributes periods of fear to not washing after bloodletting, haircuts, or nail cutting.
It also associates touching the nostrils with fear and the forehead with sleepiness.
A teaching warns that food and drink beneath a bed are affected by an evil spirit.
A baraita warns against drinking water on certain nights and attributes the danger to an evil spirit.
What does it propose for a thirsty person?
It recommends reciting a psalm with seven references to the divine voice over water.
If that psalm is unavailable, it gives an incantation instead.
With a companion present, it suggests waking the person and announcing thirst.
When alone, it suggests making a sound with the vessel or dropping something into it.
Another baraita warns against drinking from rivers or ponds at night, citing a feared blindness spirit.
What does it propose for a thirsty person in this case?
It gives a spoken warning to a companion or, alone, a progressively shortened spirit-name incantation.
Why specify four cups even for someone supported by the charity plate?
Even Rabbi Akiva, who otherwise discourages dependence, allows assistance here to publicize the miracle.
A teaching says someone with little should still mark Shabbat in a modest way at home.
What modest practice is meant?
Rav Pappa gives a small fish dish as an example.
A mishna urges energetic effort in serving God.
Rabbi Akiva begins seven instructions to his son, including avoiding distracting study locations and poorly governed cities.
His advice continues: announce entry, wear shoes, eat early, avoid financial dependence, and associate with a fortunate person.
Rav Pappa initially limits that association to partnership rather than buying and selling.
A verse about Job’s blessed work suggests benefit can flow even from a small transaction.
Buying and selling with a fortunate person can therefore also be acceptable.
The text recounts Rabbi Akiva’s imprisoned conversation with Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai about teaching despite danger.
Rabbi Akiva says he wishes to teach but fears the risks; Rabbi Shimon replies that the learner is also endangered.
Rabbi Akiva advises attributing a teaching to a great source and teaching a child from an accurate text.
A sage explains that a new learner’s first mistake is especially hard to correct.
A metaphor about reusing a pot is applied to remarriage while a former spouse lives; an alternate view begins.

112b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The prior marriage metaphor is extended with a remark that partners differ.
Rabbi Akiva praises a form of beneficial lending and marriage with children.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi warns his sons against living amid mockers in Shekhantziv.
His “Aramean bed” warning receives several readings, including a literal one tied to a later story.
He advises paying taxes and avoiding an ox emerging from a marsh.
Rabbi Shmuel limits the ox warning to a black ox in Nisan.
Rav Oshaya gives different distances from an innocuous and a repeatedly dangerous ox.
An exaggerated teaching urges retreat even if the ox seems occupied.
Rav lists calls used with an ox, lion, camel, and boat pullers.
Abaye lists practices he claims cause a skin disease.
The text explains the listed hide, fish, cup, hot water, eggs, and lice cases.
Rav Pappa advises shoes in a house with a cat, citing a feared snake bone.
An alternate version warns against entering a catless house in darkness because of snakes.
Rabbi Yishmael gives Rabbi three instructions, beginning with not harming one’s own legal position.
The first means avoiding litigation against three people who could supply opposing witnesses.
The second warns against expressing purchase interest without the means to pay.
The third advises delaying intimacy after immersion in a particular menstrual case because bleeding may recur.
Rabbi Yosei advises against solitary night travel, nakedness before a lamp, and using a new bathhouse.
How long is a bathhouse considered new?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says twelve months.
A baraita links the lamp warning to claims of epilepsy for a person or child.
Another teaching claims a child sleeping on the same bed during intimacy is affected.
The text limits that claim by the child’s age, position, and whether a hand intervenes.
A baraita attributes a nighttime warning to Agrat and destructive spirits on two nights each week.
A story says Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa restricted the alleged spirits to those nights.
A second story says Abaye forbade them entirely from inhabited areas.
The text asks why they still appear there; the answer continues on 113a.

113a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The feared appearances are explained as demons following horses on paths near the city.
Rav advises Rav Asi to choose a city with animal warnings and a leader free to govern.
Rav advises against marrying two wives, or else to marry a third.
Rav tells Rav Kahana that handling a carcass is better than breaking one’s word.
He urges paid work even when it is lowly, without invoking priestly or scholarly status.
He advises taking provisions even on a short trip to a roof.
He counsels care for cheap food as well.
Rav warns his son Chiyya against routine medicine, a dangerous jump, extracting a tooth, and provoking a snake or gentile.
A baraita lists three small beings one should not provoke.
Why should one avoid provoking them?
Their eventual power is still ahead of them.
Rav turns from unsuccessful study with his son Ayvu to practical business advice.
He advises selling goods promptly, especially wine that may spoil.
He advises collecting payment before releasing the goods.
A small reliable local profit is preferable to a larger risky one.
Dates in storage should be taken promptly to the brewery.
How many dates should one keep?
Rava sets the amount at three seah.
Rav Pappa, or in another version Rav Chisda, credits brewing with his wealth.
What does the term sudana mean?
Rav Chisda interprets it as pleasant counsel and kindness.
Rav Pappa contrasts immediate collection with the uncertainty and poor value of credit.
Rabbi Yochanan cites Jerusalem advice to leave for battle last so one can return first.
The same advice favors an ordinary Shabbat over dependence on others.
It also counsels association with someone enjoying good fortune.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites Jerusalem advice against public disgrace.
The advice urges arranging a marriage for a grown daughter.
It warns a husband to be attentive to the relationship with his first son-in-law.
What is the reason for that warning?
Rav Chisda identifies the concern as sexual misconduct.
Rav Kahana instead identifies a financial concern.
The text accepts that both concerns may apply.
Rabbi Yochanan names three kinds of people who inherit the World-to-Come.
What is distinctive about making havdala over wine?
The person saves wine from kiddush for havdala.
Rabbi Yochanan lists three people whose restraint or integrity is praised daily by God.
Rav Safra is introduced as an example of a bachelor living in a city; the story continues on 113b.

113b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Safra reacts happily when the teaching about a bachelor in a city is recited.
Rava says the praise applies instead to two cobblers who maintained restraint while serving prostitutes.
A teaching lists three dispositions beloved to God.
It then lists hypocrisy, withholding testimony, and lone testimony about sexual misconduct as hateful.
Zigud’s sole testimony against Tuveya leads Rav Pappa to punish Zigud.
Zigud objects that Tuveya sinned while he was punished.
Rav Pappa confirms that the punishment is justified.
The verse rejects a lone witness, whose report here only harms the accused person’s reputation.
Rav nevertheless permits the eyewitness to hate the sinner.
He invokes the Torah’s instruction concerning the donkey of an enemy.
Could that enemy be a gentile?
A baraita says the Torah’s enemy here is an Israelite, not a gentile.
Yet hatred of another Israelite conflicts with the Torah’s prohibition.
If witnesses had established the sin, everyone would have the same ground for hatred; why single out this person?
The case is someone who alone witnessed the misconduct.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak strengthens permission to a mitzva.
He cites the verse linking fear of God with hatred of evil.
Rav Acha asks whether the eyewitness may tell his teacher so the teacher will also hate the sinner.
Rav Ashi permits disclosure only if the teacher trusts this witness like two witnesses.
A baraita lists three dispositions that make life difficult.
Rav Yosef says that he has all three.
A teaching names groups said to dislike one another, with two added opinions.
A teaching names groups said to love one another.
A teaching lists four unbearable kinds of conduct.
Another opinion adds repeated divorce and remarriage of the same wife.
Why does the first tanna omit that additional case?
A costly marriage settlement or children may explain why the husband takes her back.
A tradition attributes five instructions to Canaan for his sons.
A teaching lists six traits of a horse, and another opinion adds a seventh.
A teaching lists people said to be ostracized by Heaven, with an added opinion about a mitzva meal.
Rav, citing Rabbi Yosei of Hutzal, asks for the source of the ban on consulting astrologers.
He cites the instruction to be wholehearted with God.
He asks for the source of honoring someone greater in even one respect.
Daniel’s superior spirit and the king’s intended appointment supply the example.
The teaching adds a restriction on intimacy after days of pure postpartum blood.
How long does the restriction last?
Rav says to wait one interval.
A baraita identifies several names for Rabbi Yosei of Hutzal.
It likewise identifies several names for Rabbi Yitzchak ben Tavla.

114a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The text identifies two names of the same Rabbi Yitzchak and supplies a mnemonic.
Rabbi Yehuda advises inexpensive food and greater spending on housing.
Ulla quotes a western proverb contrasting an extravagant meal with simple vegetables.
The mishna reports Beit Shammai’s order for the first cup: day before wine.
Beit Hillel instead put the blessing over wine before the day.
The Tosefta gives Beit Shammai’s order and two reasons: the day brings the wine and is already sanctified.
Beit Hillel give the opposite order because wine makes this kiddush possible.
Their second reason is that a frequent blessing precedes an infrequent one.
The Tosefta rules according to Beit Hillel.
Why does Beit Hillel introduce an additional reason?
It balances the two reasons offered by Beit Shammai.
The ruling for Beit Hillel is repeated.
The Gemara asks why the ruling is needed given the Divine Voice favoring Beit Hillel.
One explanation places the Tosefta before that Divine Voice.
Another follows Rabbi Yehoshua, who does not use a Divine Voice to decide law.
The next mishna begins with vegetables dipped before the seder meal.
It lists matza, bitter herbs, charoset, and two dishes, while calling charoset non-obligatory.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Tzadok disputes this and calls charoset a mitzva.
In Temple times the Paschal lamb itself was brought; the Gemara section then begins.

114b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Reish Lakish infers that performing a mitzva requires intent.
He reads the two dippings as needed because the first lettuce eating may not have been intended for maror.
The Gemara challenges how that inference follows.
Two dippings could instead be a visible difference intended to prompt children’s questions.
If so, why not teach the practice using other vegetables?
Teaching lettuce shows that even with only lettuce, two dippings create the distinction.
A baraita says one fulfills the obligation without intent, even when eating in two timely parts.
The Gemara proposes a tannaitic dispute over intent.
Rabbi Yosei requires serving lettuce again despite an earlier dipping.
Perhaps Rabbi Yosei also needs the second dipping only as a distinction for children.
That reading explains the second dipping as a visible change.
The word “mitzva” challenges that reading.
What are the two cooked dishes?
Rav Huna offers beets and rice.
Rava sought those dishes because Rav Huna had named them.
Rav Ashi infers that Rav Huna did not treat rice as a leavenable grain.
A baraita records Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri’s contrary view of rice.
Chizkiya permits fish and its attached egg as the two dishes.
Rav Yosef requires two meats to recall the Paschal and Festival offerings.
Ravina even permits meat on a bone and its cooking liquid.
With other vegetables, the first dip gets the produce blessing and the later maror gets its mitzva blessing.
How are the blessings arranged when only lettuce is available?
Rav Huna puts the produce blessing at the first eating and the maror blessing at the second.

115a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Chisda objects that one cannot eat a full portion of lettuce and only later bless the mitzva.
He places both blessings at the first lettuce eating and leaves the later eating without a blessing.
The text reports both practices and rules according to Rav Chisda.
Rav Acha sought other vegetables to avoid the dispute altogether.
A tradition attributed to Hillel warns against eating matza and maror together today.
It reasons that rabbinic maror would nullify the Torah obligation of matza.
Even a view allowing combined mitzvot may distinguish obligations of unequal legal force.
Who teaches that mitzvot do not nullify one another?
A baraita describes Hillel eating matza and maror together.
The verse speaks of eating the offering with matza and bitter herbs.
Rabbi Yochanan claims Hillel’s colleagues disagree.
He cites a baraita permitting the two foods to be eaten separately.
Rav Ashi asks why the baraita says “even” if the combined method is rejected.
Rav Ashi reads it as permitting separate eating in addition to Hillel’s combined eating.
With no decisive ruling, the practice is to eat each food with its blessing and then combine them in Temple remembrance.
Rabbi Elazar transmits a rule requiring hand washing for food dipped in liquid.
Rav Pappa begins an inference about the lettuce used at the seder, continued on 115b.

115b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Pappa infers that the lettuce must be submerged in charoset to counteract its sharpness.
Otherwise hand washing would seem unnecessary because the hands would not touch the liquid.
The lettuce may only need the aroma of charoset, without submersion.
Why then wash the hands?
Someone might nevertheless submerge the lettuce.
Rav Pappa warns against leaving maror in charoset until its bitterness is lost.
Rav Chisda teaches washing again for the second dipping.
The Sages limit that ruling to ordinary double dipping, since at the seder the first washing could be preserved.
Rav Pappa instead locates the ruling at the seder, where two dippings are prescribed.
The objection returns: why wash twice if the first washing was for this very seder?
The Haggadah and Hallel between dippings may distract the person from guarding hand purity.
Rava distinguishes swallowing matza, which counts, from swallowing maror, which lacks its required taste.
Wrapping both in palm fiber before swallowing prevents even fulfillment of matza.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi assigns each participant the foods, but removes the table only before the narrator.
Rav Huna places all the foods before the narrator; the Gemara rules like him.
Why is the table removed?
The change is meant to prompt the children to ask.
Young Abaye notices the table being taken before they have eaten and asks about it.
Rabba says Abaye’s question has served the purpose of Ma Nishtana.
Shmuel interprets “bread of affliction” as bread over which the story is answered or recited.
A baraita gives the same reading and speaks of many matters answered over it.
An alternate reading connects the spelling to the poor person’s broken piece of bread; it continues on 116a.

116a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The previous comparison concludes that matza too should be a broken piece.
Another comparison describes the poor household’s rapid oven heating and baking.
The mishna’s position that charoset is not a mitzva is recalled.
Why bring charoset if it is not a mitzva?
Rabbi Ami says it counters the sharpness of the bitter herb.
Rav Asi lists remedies for the effects of lettuce, radish, leeks, and other vegetables.
An incantation is offered while awaiting a remedy.
The mishna’s opposing view calls charoset a mitzva.
What mitzva does charoset represent?
Rabbi Levi connects it to the apple, while Rabbi Yochanan connects it to mortar.
Abaye therefore requires a tart and thick preparation to recall both.
A baraita describes spices as straw and charoset as mortar.
Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok recalls Jerusalem sellers calling the spices a mitzva.
The mishna has the second cup poured and the son ask, or be taught to ask.
Why is this night different in its use of matza?
Why are bitter herbs eaten tonight?
Why, in Temple times, was the meat roasted tonight?
Why are there two dippings tonight?
The father teaches according to the child’s understanding, from disgrace to praise, expounding the first fruits passage.
A baraita supplies other questioners if the son cannot ask, even requiring two scholars to ask each other.
The disputed mishna wording about dipping once on other nights is restated.
Rava objects that dipping once is not required on ordinary nights.
He reformulates the contrast as no obligation on other nights versus two dippings tonight.
Rav Safra challenges calling a child-prompting practice an obligation.
He restates the question as a contrast of actual practices, without claiming an ordinary-night duty.
The mishna’s instruction to start with disgrace is recalled.
What counts as the initial disgrace?
Rav begins with the ancestors’ idolatry.
Shmuel begins with slavery.
Rav Nachman asks his servant how a freed and enriched slave should respond.
The servant says to praise the master; Rav Nachman treats that as the needed question and begins with slavery.
The next mishna opens Rabban Gamliel’s teaching, continued on 116b.

116b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabban Gamliel requires naming and explaining the Paschal lamb, matza, and bitter herbs.
The Paschal lamb recalls God passing over Israelite homes.
The passage in Exodus gives the explanation for the Paschal offering.
Matza recalls the ancestors’ redemption from Egypt.
Exodus describes their baking of the dough brought out of Egypt.
Bitter herbs recall the Egyptians’ embittering of Israelite lives.
The verse describes the bitterness of forced labor.
Each generation is to see itself as personally leaving Egypt.
The verse speaks in the first person of what God did for me on leaving Egypt.
The mishna gives the Haggadah’s praise for the movement from slavery and darkness to freedom and light.
How far is Hallel recited before the meal?
Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel give different stopping points.
The section closes with redemption; Rabbi Tarfon gives a blessing without a concluding formula.
Rabbi Akiva gives an expanded blessing that closes with redemption.
Rava requires the speaker to say that God brought us out.
Rava requires lifting matza and maror, but warns against lifting meat as though it were a sacrifice outside the Temple.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov exempts a blind person from saying the Haggadah.
He links “this” in the seder verse to “this son” in the law of the rebellious son.
The blind Rav Yosef and Rav Sheshet are reported to have recited the Haggadah for their households.
Their practice is attributed to treating the present obligation as rabbinic.
Yet Rav Acha himself says the present matza obligation is rabbinic.
He still models rabbinic practice on the Torah obligation.
The same modeling should then apply to Rav Yosef and Rav Sheshet.
The word “this” is extra for the rebellious son but needed for the seder’s matza and maror, so the analogy fails.
The discussion returns to the mishna’s command to give thanks.

117a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Chisda, Rav, and Rabba disagree which praise words count as a single word.
How does Rav Chisda classify merchavya?
The question remains unresolved.
How does Rav classify Yedidya?
Rav divides it into an ordinary word and a sacred divine name.
How does Rav classify Halleluya?
Rav reports seeing the two parts written on opposite sides of a line break.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi instead interprets the term as many praises.
His own list of ten praise expressions calls Halleluya greatest because it combines name and praise.
Shmuel attributes the Song at the Sea to Moses and Israel.
Who instituted this Hallel?
Prophets established it for festivals, trouble, and subsequent redemption.
Rabbi Meir attributes all praises in Psalms to David.
He rereads a verse ending David’s prayers to include all these psalms.
Who first said this Hallel?
Rabbi Yosei favors his son’s attribution to Moses and Israel over colleagues’ attribution to David.
He argues Israel could not have celebrated Passover and Sukkot without song before David.
He also invokes the incongruity of singing Hallel while Micah’s idol stood.
Three views divide David’s psalms between personal and communal speech, with number as a clue.
The opening words of a psalm are interpreted as signs of its setting and relation to divine inspiration.
The teaching says inspiration follows joy in a mitzva rather than sadness, idleness, or frivolity.
Elisha’s request for a musician illustrates inspiration through music.
Rav applies joy to teaching law; Rav Nachman applies it to a good dream.
Another teaching and homiletic reading demand bitterness from a scholar before his teacher.
One distinction assigns joy to the teacher and awe to the student.
Another assigns joy before teaching and seriousness after beginning.
Rabba’s humorous opening followed by solemn teaching illustrates the second distinction.
A baraita asks who first said Hallel.
Rabbi Eliezer places it with Moses and Israel at the sea, answered by the Divine Spirit.
Rabbi Yehuda places it with Joshua against the Canaanite kings.
Rabbi Elazar HaModai places it with Deborah and Barak against Sisera.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya places it with Hezekiah against Sennacherib.
Rabbi Akiva places it with Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah against Nebuchadnezzar.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili places it with Mordecai and Esther against Haman.
The Sages say prophets established Hallel for recurring seasons, danger, and deliverance.
Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna dispute whether Halleluya ends or starts a psalm.
A manuscript putting it between chapters suggests uncertainty.
Rav Chanin identifies three places where it clearly opens the next psalm.
Biblical experts add two more openings.
The Gemara proposes that differing stopping points for Hallel reflect the chapter-boundary dispute.
A baraita places both schools’ stopping points at the opening of the next passage.

117b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Do the mishna and baraita differ over whether Halleluya opens or closes a psalm?
Rav Chisda reads both as closing the psalm, with “until” inclusive in one source.
The Gemara asks why that source did not specify the relevant Halleluya; the difficulty stands.
Rabba bar Rav Huna reads both as opening the next psalm, with “until” exclusive in one source.
The same wording problem challenges his explanation as well.
Rava distinguishes the redemption blessing in Shema and Hallel from the prayer blessing.
Why is the prayer formula different?
Prayer is a request for future mercy.
Rabbi Zeira similarly distinguishes the kiddush and prayer formulations for sanctification.
Why do the formulations differ?
Prayer asks for future mercy.
Rav Acha requires mentioning the Exodus in Shabbat kiddush.
He connects the command to remember the Exodus with the command to remember Shabbat.
Rabba bar Sheila distinguishes the closing formulas of prayer and haftara.
The promise of a great name for David is linked to “Shield of David.”
Reish Lakish links the patriarchal names in the first prayer blessing to God’s words to Abraham.
Should the blessing also conclude with all three patriarchs?
The verse singles out Abraham for the conclusion.
Rava reports the elders’ formulas for Shabbat and Festival prayer and kiddush.
Rava proposes a different pattern for prayer, keeping the elders’ kiddush formulas.
He explains the elders’ formulas by the fixed timing of Shabbat and Israel’s role in setting festivals.
He explains his own formulas by prayer’s communal and kiddush’s personal setting.
Both prayer and kiddush can be said either alone or with others.
Rava appeals to each practice’s usual setting.
A leader uses the elders’ formula before Rava without correction, suggesting Rava retracted.
Rav Pappa praises another leader who uses that formula.
Mareimar stops a congregation from silencing a leader and explicitly endorses the elders’ formula.
The mishna assigns Grace After Meals to the third cup and Hallel to the fourth, restricting drinking between them.
Does the third cup prove that Grace After Meals always requires wine?
Rava says the four cups are set for freedom, with a separate mitzva attached to each.
The fourth cup’s Hallel and blessing of song are recalled for the next discussion.

118a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What is the blessing of song said over the fourth cup?
Rav Yehuda names Yehallelukha; Rabbi Yochanan names Nishmat Kol Chai.
A baraita adds Great Hallel to the fourth cup, while another opinion cites Psalm 23.
Where does Great Hallel begin?
Three sages give different starting verses, ending before “By the rivers of Babylon.”
Why is it called Great Hallel?
Rabbi Yochanan points to God’s feeding of every creature.
What do its twenty-six thanks correspond to?
They correspond to generations sustained before the Torah was given.
Rav Chisda interprets divine goodness as a proportionate reckoning with each person.
Rabbi Yochanan compares the hardship of sustenance with childbirth using related words in Genesis.
He compares sustenance with redemption, distinguishing God’s provision from an angel’s rescue.
Adam’s reaction to thorns and then to bread by his own labor illustrates the burden of food.
Reish Lakish says the first condition might have been preferable and has not entirely vanished.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya compares sustaining a person with splitting the sea.
He relies on the adjacent verses about food and the sea in Great Hallel.
He also compares a difficult bodily function with death and the sea.
Adjacent verses about release and the surging sea ground that comparison.
He equates contempt for festivals with idolatry.
The ban on molten gods is followed by the command to keep the matza festival.
He condemns slander, accepting slander, and false testimony.
Adjacent verses about casting to dogs and false reports support the saying.
Why recite the ordinary Hallel if Great Hallel exists?
The ordinary Hallel mentions five key events or hopes.
Verses are supplied for the Exodus, sea, Torah, resurrection, and messianic travail.
Rabbi Yochanan and an alternate version connect “Not to us” to oppression or Gog and Magog.
Rav Nachman adds the rescue of righteous souls from Gehenna as another reason for this Hallel.
Chizkiya adds the furnace rescue of three righteous men.
Their descent into the furnace is mapped to verses they each recited.
Their ascent is mapped to the verses of Psalm 117.
Another opinion assigns one verse to Gabriel.
A story says God reserved Abraham’s rescue for Himself but promised Gabriel a later rescue.
The promised case is the three men cast into Nebuchadnezzar’s furnace.
Gabriel argues that a fire angel cooling fire would show greater divine power than hail extinguishing it; the account continues.

118b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gabriel proposes a miracle within the furnace and is permitted to descend, then praises God.
Rabbi Natan instead assigns that praise verse to the fish of the sea.
A midrash describes Israel’s fear that Egyptians survived on the other shore.
God commands the sea to release the Egyptians and promises a larger future return.
The Kishon River is named guarantor of that promise.
The sea releases the bodies, and a verse says Israel saw them on the shore.
What does one and a half times their number mean?
The numbers of Pharaoh’s and Sisera’s chariots are six hundred and nine hundred.
The battle with Sisera drives his iron-equipped troops into the Kishon River.
Kishon sweeps them into the sea in payment of its guarantee.
The verse says the Kishon swept them away.
Why is Kishon called the ancient river?
It had guaranteed the ancient promise; the fish then recite the praise verse.
Reish Lakish interprets the barren woman verse as Israel’s complaint of neglect.
Rava reads the love verse as Israel’s plea that God hear its supplications.
He reads the lowliness verse as a plea for rescue despite few mitzvot.
Rav Kahana introduces teachings sent by the ill Rabbi Yishmael in his father’s name.
Why would the nations praise God for mercy shown to Israel?
The nations praise wonders they witnessed; Israel has still greater reason to praise.
A teaching imagines Egypt’s gift to the Messiah being accepted for its former hospitality.
Kush argues that its gift should also be accepted, and God agrees.
Rome claims the same by kinship, but a verse tells Gabriel to rebuke it.
An alternate reading identifies the reed beast with a pig-like ravager.
Rabbi Yochanan reads the beast and bulls as an indictment of Rome’s conduct and violence.
The silver phrase is read as officials taking payment without fulfilling obligations.
The scattering phrase is read as exile brought on by desired intimacies.
Another teaching describes Rome’s markets, towers, floors, and immense food stores.
For whom are the stores intended?
They are said to be for Israel’s scholars, supported by Isaiah’s promise.
What does “not be treasured” mean?
Rav Yosef distinguishes a storehouse from a hidden treasury.
What does “those who dwell before God” mean? Rabbi Elazar’s answer begins on 119a.

119a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Elazar identifies one who knows or greets a colleague’s place in the study hall.
What does the verse’s phrase about stately clothing mean?
One reading praises concealing matters God concealed, namely Torah secrets.
Another praises revealing concealed reasons for Torah laws.
Rav Kahana reads “for the victor” as praise of God, who rejoices when prevailed upon.
Moses averting destruction of Israel illustrates that reading.
A reading of Ezekiel asks why “hand” is written singular beneath the living beings’ wings.
It depicts God’s hand sheltering penitents from strict judgment.
Shmuel says Joseph collected the world’s wealth into Egypt.
A verse says Joseph gathered the money in Egypt and Canaan.
Where is the evidence for wealth from other lands?
A second verse says all the land came to Egypt.
Israel is then said to have taken that wealth out at the Exodus.
Rav Asi and Rabbi Shimon picture Egypt emptied like a trap or sea without contents.
The treasure stays until Shishak takes it from Rehoboam.
The Kings passage reports Shishak taking Temple and royal treasures.
The treasure passes through Zerah, Asa, Hadrimmon, Ammon, and Jehoshaphat.
It then passes through later kings and empires until Rome.
Rabbi Chama describes three treasures Joseph hid, one reserved for the future righteous.
Reish Lakish identifies the harmful stored wealth in Ecclesiastes with Korah’s.
A verse about wealth at their feet is read as money supporting a person.
Rabbi Levi describes the immense load of keys to Korah’s stores.
A mnemonic introduces a return to the Hallel verses and their speakers.
The verse of thanks is attributed to David.
The rejected-stone verse is attributed to Jesse.
The verse about the Lord’s deed is attributed to David’s brothers.
The day the Lord made is attributed to Samuel.
The plea for rescue is attributed to David’s brothers.
The plea for prosperity is attributed to David.
The blessing for one who comes in God’s name is attributed to Jesse.
The blessing from God’s house is attributed to Samuel.
All recite the verse about God giving light.
Samuel recites the festival-procession verse.
David recites his personal thanks.
All recite the final exaltation.
A mishna about local Hallel practice is introduced and continues on 119b.

119b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna makes repeating verses and the blessing after Hallel depend on local custom.
Abaye limits local choice to the final blessing; the opening blessing is required.
Shmuel’s rule places the blessing before every mitzva.
How does the expression “over” imply before performance?
A verse says Ahimaaz passed the Kushite, meaning he got ahead of him.
Abaye cites Jacob passing before his family.
An alternate proof cites the king passing before them.
A baraita says Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar ben Perata repeated verses in Hallel.
What did Rabbi Elazar add?
Abaye says he added repetitions from “I will give thanks” onward.
Rav Avira asks how to read the verse about Isaac being weaned.
It is read as a future feast when God extends mercy to Isaac’s descendants.
At the feast Abraham declines the blessing cup because Ishmael came from him.
Isaac declines because Esau came from him.
Jacob declines because he married two sisters.
Moses declines because he did not enter the Land of Israel.
Joshua declines because he had no son, as inferred from a genealogy.
David accepts and cites the verse about lifting the cup of salvation.
The mishna forbids an afikoman after the Paschal lamb.
What does afikoman mean here?
Rav reads it as leaving one Paschal group for another.
Shmuel and others read it as dessert or specified after-meal foods.
A baraita supports the reading that bans dates, roasted grains, and nuts afterward.
Shmuel also forbids an afikoman after matza.
The mishna specifies the Paschal lamb, seemingly allowing it after matza.
The prohibition after mild-tasting matza is obvious; the mishna adds even the stronger-tasting lamb.
A Tosefta allows other cakes before a final olive-bulk of matza; its inference continues on 120a.

120a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Tosefta says matza may come last even after other food, though a full stomach might have suggested otherwise.
Mar Zutra transmits an alternate version of Shmuel’s afikoman ruling.
The mishna’s restriction after the lamb is proposed as support for eating afterward with matza.
The Gemara reads the mishna as mentioning the lamb in addition to the obvious case of matza.
The Tosefta’s final olive-bulk of matza is raised as an objection.
It permits matza even after other foods, when one might eat too much.
Rava holds matza remains a Torah obligation today, while maror is rabbinic.
Why does maror differ?
Its verse ties it to the Paschal offering, which is absent today.
The same verse also mentions matza.
A separate verse repeats the command to eat matza in the evening.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov instead makes both present obligations rabbinic.
How does he account for the separate matza verse?
It requires matza for the impure and distant traveler even when they miss the offering.
Rava says that case needs no separate verse because they are no worse than the uncircumcised.
A baraita excludes an uncircumcised man from the lamb but includes him in matza and maror.
Rav Acha treats the two cases as requiring separate teachings.
A baraita supports Rava: matza on the later days is optional, like the seventh day.
The singled-out seventh day teaches the rule for the rest of the festival.
Could even the first night be optional?
The verse about eating with matza and maror establishes its obligation with the offering.
What establishes the first-night duty without the Temple?
The separate evening verse obligates matza even then.
The next mishna distinguishes some diners sleeping from the whole group sleeping.

120b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna distinguishes dozing from sleep and gives impurity rules for leftover and invalid offerings.
Rabbi Yosei’s distinction between dozing and full sleep is repeated.
What counts as dozing?
Rav Ashi describes partial awareness, answering when called but unable to reason fully.
Rabba tells Abaye that he was dozing, so eating may continue under the mishna.
The midnight impurity rule implies that the Paschal lamb becomes leftover then.
Which tanna holds that view?
Rav Yosef identifies Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
His baraita connects “that night” of eating with “that night” of the Egyptian plague.
The plague’s midnight limit supplies the eating limit.
Rabbi Akiva invokes the verse about eating in haste, extending the time to dawn.
He reads “at night” as excluding daytime eating, not setting a midnight end.
What does Rabbi Akiva derive from the word “that”?
It excludes a second night, despite a possible analogy to peace-offerings.
Rabbi Elazar derives the one-night limit from the ban on leaving meat until morning.
Rabbi Akiva says “morning” alone might have meant the second morning.
Rabbi Elazar holds that an unqualified morning means the first morning.
Rava applies Rabbi Elazar’s midnight limit to matza even now.
Is that not obvious from matza’s link to the Paschal lamb?
The repeated matza verse could seem to sever the link, but it restores the original timing.
Rav Huna and Rav Chisda dispute the priestly rationale and minimum quantity for impurity of piggul and leftover meat.

121a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The two priestly concerns apply to different cases, piggul and leftover meat.
Suspected priests explain piggul; lazy priests explain leftover meat.
The sages also give different minimum sizes, olive-bulk and egg-bulk.
The olive measure follows prohibition, while the egg measure follows impurity rules.
Rabbi Yishmael says the Paschal blessing covers the Festival offering, but not the reverse.
Rabbi Akiva says neither offering’s blessing covers the other.
Rabbi Yishmael includes sprinkling within pouring, but not pouring within sprinkling.
Rabbi Akiva treats pouring and sprinkling as distinct in both directions.

121b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Simlai is asked about blessings at a firstborn son’s redemption.
The father clearly recites the blessing over the redemption mitzva.
Who recites Shehecheyanu, the priest or the father?
The priest receives the redemption payment and its benefit.
The father is the one performing the mitzva.
Rabbi Simlai takes the unresolved question to the study hall.
The scholars say the father recites both blessings.
The final ruling confirms that the father recites both.
The chapter and tractate of Pesachim close.
